evals.prompt: We run PortoBuild, an annual developer conference in Porto, about 900 attendees, fourth edition wrapped two weeks ago. Our Discord (about 1,400 members, carried over from the conference) goes dead for most of the year. The team is buzzing right now and we've drafted a content calendar: twelve monthly themes (January is 'CI/CD month', February is 'observability month', and so on), each with weekly discussion prompts, a monthly live AMA, and new topic sub-channels. Everyone on the team is a volunteer with a day job; realistically after October nobody has hours until we start planning the next edition in spring. Can you review the plan and tell us what to post?
evals.expected_output: A between-editions cadence plan that rejects the twelve-theme calendar, chooses a posture the team's real quiet-months capacity can hold (dormant-but-open or a light pulse), names an owner, and includes a dated dormancy notice or a pulse plan fed from existing material.
expectations: Rejects or substantially scales back the twelve-theme monthly calendar rather than refining, filling in, or endorsing it.
Grounds the cadence choice in who has recurring hours in the quiet months, not in the team's current post-edition enthusiasm.
Identifies the proposed plan (live AMAs, new sub-channels, standing prompts) as the heaviest cadence posture, which requires funded or guaranteed moderation capacity this volunteer team lacks.
Recommends dormant-but-open, or at most a light occasional pulse, as the posture for this team.
States that a recurring digest or spotlight rhythm is only viable when one named person holds recurring hours across the whole gap, and lapses otherwise.
Names, or requires the team to name, a single owner for the chosen posture, and states that a cadence with no named owner is not a decided posture.
Warns that a published calendar the team then abandons reads worse to members than deliberate, stated silence.
If dormancy is chosen, prescribes one pinned dated notice containing a date tied to the next build-up, a named owner, a conduct-report route that still works, and a promise small enough to keep.
States that dormancy keeps the archive readable and the member list intact and owned; it is not deleting or closing the server.
Any pulse plan proposed fills its slots from material that already exists (edition recordings, members' own posts) rather than requiring original content per slot.
Treats missed posting cycles as a signal to demote the cadence next gap, not as a team-discipline problem to push through.
Requires the member list to have a named owner and a written retention decision at the start of the gap, whatever cadence is chosen.
Does not set message-volume, engagement-rate, or activity targets for the space as success measures.

evals.prompt: Priya founded DataPipe Conf (annual, Bengaluru, six editions) and is stepping down at the end of next month. The community Slack, 2,100 members, is a workspace registered under her personal Gmail. She has already added Arjun, next year's lead, as a workspace admin, so we think access is sorted. Our team charter says leadership handovers run 6 to 12 months, so we were planning to stretch the community-platform transfer across the next year too. Priya also has the only export of the member email list on her laptop. She's a volunteer like the rest of us. What else should we tick off before she goes?
evals.expected_output: A community-asset handoff plan that transfers ownership of record first, refuses to borrow the team charter's 6-12-month window for the platform, inventories every asset with holder-today and holder-after, restates the member-list retention decision, and is dated with a review date.
expectations: Identifies that adding Arjun as admin while the workspace stays registered to Priya's personal account leaves the space unrecoverable the day that account closes, so access is not sorted.
Requires transferring ownership of record of the workspace first, before rearranging admin roles.
Requires adding a second admin who is neither Priya nor Arjun, so the handoff does not produce a bus factor of one.
Rejects stretching the platform transfer across the charter's 6-12-month window, on the grounds that window covers the lead role while the platform account's timeframe is a separate deliberate call.

Prescribes a one-page written inventory listing each asset (workspace ownership, admin and moderator roles, billing, domain or vanity links, standing invite links, member-list export, archive, conduct reporting route) with a holder today and a holder after per row.
Treats any inventory row with no holder-after as the finding to resolve, not a blank to leave.
Requires the member-list export to move off Priya's laptop, with its format, location, and consent basis recorded and a named person able to reach it.

Restates the member-list retention decision explicitly at the handoff (named living owner, what members were told when they joined, permitted scope, a review-or-deletion date) rather than letting it be inherited by silence.
Checks that the conduct-reporting route resolves to someone who will still be reading it after Priya leaves.
Prescribes posting to the space, in the event's established voice, that ownership of the space and the data has changed.
Dates the handoff document and sets a next review date.
Frames the handoff as something a departing volunteer will want to complete, not as an employee offboarding procedure with enforceable obligations.
Runs the transfer as a session with both people present, filling the inventory together, not as a document sent to the person leaving.
Separates the community-asset transfer from the team/decision-rights handover and from the operational learning log, treating them as distinct artifacts rather than one bundle.

evals.prompt: GridForge Summit is our annual open-source energy-software conference in Berlin, about 1,200 people. Community members in Lisbon, Krakow and Zagreb have each asked to run 'GridForge Lisbon' style local editions under our banner, and honestly it sounds like free growth. Can you draft the chapter program for us: chapter-lead application form, brand usage guidelines, quality standards for local events, and a plan to keep those local groups engaged in our Discord between summits?
evals.expected_output: An answer that splits the request in two, declines the chapter/brand-licensing half as out of scope, and delivers only the engagement half: per-city threads on the existing surface, a named local member per city, the same content feed, one member list under one retention decision.
expectations: Applies the decisive test of whether anyone outside the organizing team would run an event under the event's name, and classifies the chapter request as governance and brand licensing.
Declines to draft the chapter-lead application form, brand usage guidelines, and local-event quality standards, rather than producing them.
States plainly that licensing the brand to independently-run local editions is a gap it has no playbook for, instead of quietly improvising an answer.
Splits the request into a governance half and an engagement half, and answers only the engagement half.
The engagement half stays on the team's own surface: per-city threads or sub-spaces inside the existing Discord, run by the organizing team.
Recommends finding a named local member willing to keep each city thread warm.
Feeds the city threads the same digest and spotlight stream the main space gets, rather than inventing separate local programming.
Keeps local members in the same member list under the same retention decision, not in per-city lists.
Warns concretely that letting the brand question ride informally fails at the first incident at an event carrying the name that the team did not organize.
Does not treat 'free growth' as a reason to proceed, and makes no growth recommendation.
Does not reframe the local groups as external partner events to cross-promote with.
Tells the user explicitly which half of their request was answered and that the governance half needs a decision path this plan does not provide.

evals.prompt: ShipItCon (annual, Dublin) here. Two wins to run past you. One: we changed registration so every ticket buyer is now automatically added to our Circle community. Membership jumped from 600 to 2,900 overnight, and the sponsor prospectus now leads with 'a 2,900-member developer community'. Two: the community has been quiet since August, so our first post of the year will announce that early-bird tickets are live, ends Friday, book now, and we'll email the whole list too. Sound good?
evals.expected_output: A response that reverses both 'wins': auto-enrollment is rejected on consent grounds and the sponsor figure corrected, and the sales blast is replaced by a re-engagement touchpoint that references the past edition, makes one cheap ask, and is signed by a person.
expectations: Rejects auto-enrolling ticket buyers as community members rather than optimizing or softening it.
Gives the consent reason: the ticketing sign-up granted consent for a different purpose, and community membership was never part of what was granted.
Identifies the 2,900 figure as a manufactured membership number and flags leading the sponsor prospectus with it as misrepresentation.
Recommends an opt-in path into the community for ticket buyers instead of automatic enrollment.
Rejects 'tickets are live, ends Friday, book now' as the first contact after months of silence.
Explains the specific damage of the sales blast: it converts the warmest people who were coming anyway, and teaches everyone else the space only contacts them to sell.
The replacement first contact references something that happened (the edition they attended, what members shipped), because members have a memory of the past edition and none of the announced one.
The replacement makes one low-cost ask that is not 'buy', such as answering a call for talks, naming a topic, or saying whether they are coming.
The replacement is signed by a named person and written in the event's established voice.
States that contact with the attendee list rides on the consent basis it was collected under, an inherited duty, not a fresh policy invented for the community.
Requires correcting the membership number given to sponsors to genuinely opted-in members, not keeping 2,900 with a caveat.

evals.prompt: KernelDays is a systems-programming conference that runs once a year in Helsinki. To keep our forum alive between editions we're building a points system: badges for posting, a monthly leaderboard, levels that unlock a 'Community Champion' title, and we'll feature the top three champions with photos on the conference homepage. A volunteer already built a prototype bot. We also want the ladder to eventually feed people toward helping organize. Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the points/leaderboard scheme with the three reasons it fails an annual-cycle audience, replaced by a small named-step ladder whose rungs are asynchronously climbable, with consent gates on public naming and the organizer-candidate endpoint routed out.
expectations: Rejects the points, badges, and leaderboard scheme for an audience that meets once a year, rather than tuning its parameters.
States that the scheme measures posting volume, which is not the outcome the space exists for (people returning to the next edition, some bringing work).
States that the scheme rewards the loudest members rather than the returning ones.
States that the scheme demands maintenance in exactly the months the team has no hours.
Replaces it with a small ladder of named steps (attendee, regular, contributor shaped), each step with a stated way in and a stated reward.
Requires every step above the first to be climbable entirely asynchronously, because an annual event gives one live touch per year.
Requires each step's way in to work without personally knowing an organizer, so the ladder is not a clique with a diagram.
Requires asking consent before publishing anyone's name or photo as a champion or regular, with an opt-out that needs no explanation.
Routes the 'feed people toward helping organize' endpoint to the team-structure candidate flag, and stops the ladder there rather than building organizer recruitment into the community mechanism.
Scopes the mechanism to non-volunteer members, with volunteer recognition handled by its own separate loop.
Reports ladder movement as a raw count of members who moved a step, never as a rate or percentage.
Ties success to attendees returning next edition rather than to posting frequency, streaks, or leaderboard positions.

evals.prompt: Our board asked for community KPIs for RustReef (annual conference, 2,800 attendees, 3,100-member Slack). Draft proposal: (a) daily active members and monthly message volume as the headline numbers; (b) we read that the events industry's blended retention rate is barely above 30 percent, so we'll commit to beating it with a 45 percent return-rate target next edition; (c) a community consultant told us healthy communities follow the 5/12/45 group-size thresholds, and with only about 50 people talking out of 3,100 we're failing badly and need an activation push. Can you finalize the KPI sheet?
evals.expected_output: A KPI sheet centered on carry rate as a self-set threshold plus three binary gates, with the 30 percent industry figure demoted to context, the 5/12/45 numbers corrected and ruled inapplicable to a member list, and the activation push rejected.
expectations: Rejects daily active members and message volume as headline KPIs, naming the failure: they measure the space, not whether the edition's audience returns.
Makes the share of one edition's attendees who register for the next one (carry rate) the central outcome number.
Treats the roughly 30 percent blended industry retention figure as evidence that return rates run lower than teams assume, and explicitly not as a target or baseline to beat.
Notes that the blended figure mixes every event type, none of them a technical conference, so it cannot anchor a commitment.
Requires the carry-rate threshold to be self-set and fixed before the gap starts, not derived from the industry figure or set after the data arrives.
Identifies 5/12/45 as a misquote of the community-size threshold series (the actual sequence being 7, 13, 50, 90, 150).
States that those thresholds describe groups with ongoing interaction and say nothing about a member list, which is a stock, not a group.
States that around 50 active talkers out of 3,100 members is a normal shape for an event's space, not a failure, and rejects the activation-push premise.
Includes a binary gate for cadence kept: posts planned versus posts actually made across the gap, on the chosen posture.
Includes a binary gate for list integrity: a named owner and a written retention decision for the member list on the day the gap starts.
Includes a binary gate for handoff readiness: a dated access document naming a living holder for every account, checked on a schedule.
Positions the carry rate as evidence handed onward to the demand/market-fit read, not as a growth recommendation the community plan itself makes.
Labels every threshold on the sheet as self-set rather than presenting any as an industry benchmark.

evals.prompt: Two things for FjordSec, our annual security conference in Oslo. First: on stage we're quite formal, sober and precise, no memes, but that feels heavy for the Discord in the off months, so we want to write a second, cosier 'off-season voice' guide for the community mods: more casual, more emoji, more banter. Second: to bridge the ten-month gap we'd like to run a small quarterly meetup, a borrowed office, 40 seats, one invited speaker each time. Can you write the voice guide and sketch the quarterly format?
evals.expected_output: A refusal on both counts: the off-season voice is written as a delta against the fixed register rather than a second voice, and the quarterly meetup is routed out as an event property, with in-scope gap-bridging alternatives offered instead.
expectations: Refuses to author a second, separate off-season voice guide.
States the principle that the event's identity or register is fixed and only its expression modulates between editions.
Prescribes a delta document mapping each existing register attribute to its between-editions expression, instead of a standalone tone guide.
Covers the hardest rows of that delta: what the register sounds like when nothing has happened, and when the news is somebody else's.
Requires the existing register as input, and if none has been decided, routes to fix that first, labeling anything written before it as provisional.
Declines to sketch the quarterly meetup format.
Gives the reason: a touchpoint that needs a venue, a schedule, or an invited speaker is an event property, not a between-editions community tactic.
Routes the quarterly-meetup question to the portfolio-level property decision rather than answering it inside the community plan.
Offers in-scope gap-bridging alternatives on the existing surface (a digest, a member spotlight, discussion threads) that need no venue, schedule, or speaker.
Does not offer the cosy second voice as a compromise, pilot, or A/B option alongside the recommendation.
Presents the between-editions expression for approval before the mods change anything members can see.

evals.prompt: CloudCamp Antwerp wrapped in September. The edition comms team archived the attendee announcement channels on their published wind-down date and left #general plus the per-team project channels running; that's now mine to run until next summer. Three questions. One: can I reorganize the surviving channels? I'd fold the small per-project channels into #general to tidy up, and I think their wind-down archived some channels too aggressively, so I want to restore two. Two: about 60 past volunteers are in the space, and I'd like to build them a recognition program with a dedicated volunteers server. Three: next edition's comms lead asked what I'll give them at build-up, and I said 'the Discord will still be there'. Anything wrong with that?
evals.expected_output: An answer that keeps the per-project channels, refuses to reverse the wind-down, routes volunteer recognition to its own loop as a segment inside the existing surface, and replaces 'the Discord will still be there' with a live member-list handback carrying consent basis and reachable count.
expectations: Rejects folding the per-project channels into #general, because a returning member reopens the channel scoped to their project and the general channel does not replace that.
Refuses to restore the two archived channels or otherwise reverse the edition team's wind-down decisions; the between-editions role starts where wind-down ended.
Does not redesign the edition's channel roster or routing rules in any other way.
Declines to build the volunteer recognition program, because the volunteer alumni loop (list, thank-you, candidate flag) belongs to its own owner, not to the community role.
Rejects a dedicated second volunteers server; past volunteers run as a segment inside the existing surface.
Scopes the between-editions programming audience to non-volunteer members.
States that 'the Discord will still be there' is not a handback.
Specifies the handback as a live member list: who joined, on what consent basis, and who is actually reachable.
Times the handback to the next edition's build-up, when the new edition's channels open.
Establishes the user as the named owner of the space for the gap, with the conduct-report route stated as still monitored.
Requires the member list's owner and retention decision to be settled now, at the start of the gap, not at handback.
Frames the role as two handovers: receiving the space at wind-down and returning the live list at build-up.

evals.prompt: For NimbusFest (annual, Toronto, fifth edition coming), our long-standing hygiene practice is to delete the community Slack about a month after each edition and spin up a fresh workspace the next spring: clean slate, no stale channels, and our privacy-minded co-organizer likes that it 'solves data retention automatically'. This year someone objected, so before we delete: how long are we actually allowed to keep member data under PIPEDA? If you know the exact retention period, put it in our policy doc along with the deletion date.
evals.expected_output: A response that stops the delete-and-reopen cycle for a recurring event, refuses to quote any jurisdiction's retention period and routes that ruling to counsel, and writes the retention decision as four fields with a concrete review date.
expectations: Rejects deleting and reopening the workspace each edition for a recurring event, rather than endorsing it as hygiene.
States what deletion actually discards: the member list and the archive, which are the community asset itself.
Notes that export-plus-deletion is a legitimate end state only for a one-off edition, not a recurring event.
Rejects 'deletion solves data retention automatically': a retention decision is a deliberate written artifact, not a side effect of clean-up.
Declines to quote a PIPEDA retention period, or any jurisdiction's, and does not write one into the policy doc.
Routes the actual retention ruling to the organizer's own counsel.
Prescribes the retention decision as four fields: a named living owner, the basis in the words members were told at join, the permitted scope, and a review-or-deletion date.
Distinguishes scope grants: 'announcing our own next edition' and 'anything the team decides later' are different scopes, and only the one granted applies.
States that the retention duty is inherited from the sign-up and attendee-list consent framework, to be restated, not re-derived as a second policy.
Requires the review-or-deletion date to be a concrete date, not 'when it stops being useful'.
Presents the dormant alternative: archive readable, member list intact and owned, one dated notice, at near-zero effort, so deletion is not the cheap option it looks like.
Requires the retention decision to be restated at every future handoff rather than inherited silently.
